articles.title: Et tu, Fedorov? The betrayal of Volodymyr Zelensky.
articles.summary: Mykhailo Fedorov, the country’s former defense minister and a longtime political ally of Zelensky, called for a legal way to be found for Ukraine to hold wartime elections, even though the nation’s constitution forbids it.
articles.body:
No, it was not the Ides of March. But Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky could be forgiven if Aug. 18 felt like it.

Mykhailo Fedorov, the country’s former defense minister and a longtime political ally of Zelensky, called for a legal way to be found for Ukraine to hold wartime elections , even though the nation’s constitution forbids it.

Fedorov’s symbolic knife, delivered via a post on his newly created YouTube account, was aimed straight at Zelensky’s back. Zelensky had sacked Fedorov over a leadership dispute with the now departed Col. Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi. He had been the commander-in-chief of Ukraine’s military.

Fedorov’s abrupt firing led to widespread protests in support of the 35-year-old, who had been widely credited with Ukraine’s turnaround on the battlefield and for expanding and accelerating the fight deep inside Russia , which is ravaging its oil and gas sector and its military supply chain while isolating Russian forces in occupied Crimea.

In making his bombshell case for wartime elections, Fedorov argued, “We must not let [Russian President Vladimir] Putin decide when Ukrainians can choose their government.” To say the least, that is a straw man argument.

Putin is not stopping Ukrainians from voting. Ukraine’s constitution is the obstacle. Article 83 clearly states that if the term of the parliament while martial law is in effect, then the parliament’s powers are automatically extended until after martial law is ended.

The Ukrainian constitution also prohibits constitutional amendments during periods of martial law. So the only way to hold an election would be for Zelensky to end martial law — which would be foolhardy, given a state of war exists between Russia and Ukraine.

Fedorov’s proposal is also impractical. Even if a legal workaround could be found for the Ukrainian constitution, it would be virtually impossible to hold a safe, free, and fair election while the entire country is under daily Russian ballistic missile and drone attacks.

For one thing, more than 8,000 polling stations, representing one-quarter of the total, are either located in Russian-occupied Ukraine or on the front lines. Between 4 and 5 million Ukrainian citizens are caught behind Russian enemy lines. Would Fedorov simply disenfranchise them?

Ongoing air raids could wreak havoc on all the other polling stations. And at any given time, there are nearly 1 million voters serving on the frontlines in the Donbas and across southern Ukraine opposite the Crimean Peninsula. As many as 7.5 million Ukrainians are also living abroad now as refugees.

But the biggest problem is that Fedorov’s gambit risks aiding Putin , who has long claimed that Zelensky is an illegitimate president. Moscow has said repeatedly that new elections in Ukraine are a precondition for any comprehensive peace settlement or treaty between Russia and Ukraine.

Putin knows that Zelensky is his most formidable foe, Churchillian in his stature. That is why Putin has tried so hard to get rid of him, both through calls for new elections and repeated assassination attempts .

Wittingly or not, Fedorov is also strengthening the hand of Vice President JD Vance, whose strong dislike of Zelensky is widely known. Vance has frequently criticized Ukraine’s approach to its war of self-defense against Russia. In a February 2025 meeting in the Oval Office, Vance famously accused Zelensky of ingratitude toward the U.S.

Only last week, Vance succeeded in pressuring Zelensky to lay off with drone strikes against Russian oil tankers, in order to help stabilize global oil prices and protect U.S. companies. Zelensky likely agreed only in order to ensure that Ukraine remains on track to receive a license to produce Patriot missile interceptors.

By effectively doing Vance’s bidding, Fedorov is also foolishly undermining the improvement in personal relations between Zelensky and President Trump. In early July, during a NATO meeting in Ankara, Turkey, Trump praised Zelensky and announced that he supports Ukraine getting the Patriot license.

Fedorov’s timing is clear enough. Zelensky’s poll numbers are not good. In hypothetical match-ups , he is running neck-and-neck with Fedorov and Valeriy Zaluzhnyi, the former commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Notably, Zelensky would be expected to lose a hypothetical runoff against either man.

That is why this looks and feels like an opportunistic “Et tu, Brute?” moment, straight out of William Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar.

Yet, this time it might have a very different ending. Early reaction in Kyiv — and it could still change — is that Fedorov overplayed his hand, that his ambition and lack of patience perhaps got the better of him.

Fedorov must back down and close ranks. Ukraine continues to be under daily heavy ballistic missile and drone attack by Russia. The war hangs in the balance. The last thing Ukraine needs ahead of winter is a dead or badly wounded Caesar.

Mark Toth writes on national security and foreign policy. Col. (Ret.) Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the U.S. European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. They are the cofounders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.

articles.title: Pennsylvania State Police helicopter violently collides with plane, pilot dead: FAA
articles.summary: Two people were aboard the PSP aircraft when it collided with a Cessna 150 around 6:50 p.m., a Federal Aviation Administration spokesperson said in a statement.
articles.body:
CARLISLE, Pa. ( WHTM ) – An airplane and Pennsylvania State Police helicopter collided violently at the Carlisle Airport located in Carlisle, Pennsylvania, Wednesday evening, federal authorities confirmed to Nexstar’s WHTM.

Two people were aboard the PSP helicopter when it collided with a Cessna 150 around 6:50 p.m., a Federal Aviation Administration spokesperson said in a statement. The plane was descending onto the runway and veered into the helicopter, according Lt. Col. George Bivens, Pennsylvania’s acting state police commissioner.

The pilot of the plane was killed. Officials aren’t releasing their identity until family is informed.

“When I say it was a very violent crash, that plane was cut into a lot of pieces,” Bivens said Wednesday night.

Bivens explained that the Cessna, a two-seat aircraft, is typically used for training purposes. He also confirmed the pilot was performing a training exercise.

Both of the pilots in the helicopter were trapped until one pushed out a window and helped the other out through the window, said Bivens.

Gov. Josh Shapiro, who rushed to the incident, issued a statement, saying: “Tonight could’ve been much worse. Tonight could’ve been much more tragic for our state police family.”

The NTSB will lead an investigation along with the FAA, the agency confirmed.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Will Democrats abandon Florida after Nixon win?
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Democrats face uphill fight in Florida ▪ Cassidy shares doubts on FDA nominee ▪ Trump downplays bond market concerns ▪ Melanoma mRNA vaccine trial success Florida Democrats are warning national party members not to abandon the state in November after democratic socialist Angie Nixon defeated moderate Alex Vindman in a shocking…
articles.body:
▪ Democrats face uphill fight in Florida

Florida Democrats are warning national party members not to abandon the state in November after democratic socialist Angie Nixon defeated moderate Alex Vindman in a shocking upset in Tuesday’s Democratic Senate primary.

Shortly after Nixon’s victory, Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved the Florida Senate race from “likely Republican” to “safe Republican.”

“This was always going to be a heavy lift for Democrats, but following the primary, we are moving Florida’s Senate race back to Safe Republican,” Sabato’s Crystal Ball’s analysis read .

The election handicapper noted the “silver lining” for Democrats is that donors might be less inclined to waste money on a state that Democrats have struggled to win in recent years. The party last won a federal statewide race in 2012.

“While it is impossible to precisely dictate where donors send money, those contributions would presumably be more likely to end up in more competitive states,” the analysis added.

Several Democratic strategists in Florida, however, warned of long-term implications of reallocating resources in interviews with Morning Report.

Democratic strategist Steve Schale — who ran former President Obama ’s Florida operation for his 2008 campaign and was a senior adviser for the 2012 campaign — said it would be a mistake for Democrats to sleep on the state altogether.

He noted more congressional seats are likely to shift south after the next census and that Democrats need Florida to win control of the House.

“It’s hard for me to see a world where we get to 218 in the House with any regularity if we’re not winning districts on the I-4 corridor in Florida and winning seats in Miami, and right now we’re not,” Schale said.

He also warned of “downballot implications” of not investing in the state.

“I worry if Democrats don’t think the top of the ticket’s worth investing in, it makes it a lot harder for those folks running down the ballot to have kind of the baseline they need to win.”

Fernand Amandi , a Miami-based pollster and consultant whose firm also helped Obama’s campaign win the state in 2008 and 2012, called Florida “a state that you have to engage in if you ever hope to win the White House in the future again.”

“Part of the reason that Donald Trump has won reelection twice, in my opinion, and why the MAGA movement has grown is because Florida was basically left all alone by the Democrats and disregarded,” Amandi said.

He also noted how important Florida is to the Make America Great Again movement.

“It’s the head of the snake of the MAGA movement, where they literally all live, at least the main leaders of the party,” Amandi added. “ And it’s the laboratory for exporting MAGA concepts throughout the rest of the country in Florida.”

Sharon Wright Austin — a professor at the University of Florida, who serves as vice president and president-elect of the National Conference of Black Political Scientists — said it “would be the ultimate slap in the face for Black female voters” if national Democrats decide not to invest resources in the Senate race now that Nixon is the nominee.

“I think that it’s going to really be a wake-up call and make people who are Black Democrats really take some time to think about whether or not we should continue to support white Democrat candidates,” she said, adding, “O r maybe we should just not continue to support the Democratic Party if they’re not supporting us.”

Schale said he’s “skeptical” national Democrats would have invested many resources in Florida, even if Vindman had won the primary.

He said he has talked to fellow Democrats involved on the national level, and “ having been through a few of these rodeos with those guys, I just, I don’t believe establishment institutional Democratic world was going to be here.”

Schale noted that Democrats who hope to win statewide races in Florida will need to shrink the GOP turnout advantage, win independents by 20 to 25 points and perform better among Republican voters than their GOP opponents do among Democrats.

“I think the math is hard for Angie, I do, but, in all fairness, if you and I had this same conversation and Alex Vindman had won, I would be telling you the exact same thing,” he said.

Amandi said whether Nixon has a shot in November will depend on whether she distances herself from the democratic socialist label. Nixon officially joined the Democratic Socialists of America just a few weeks before her primary win.

“The problem with the DSA is that, for all of their respectable economic populist positions, there are some not-so-much talked about elements of the DSA blanket platform that are not just problematic or unacceptable; they’re disqualifying nonstarters for huge swaths of the Florida electorate,” Amandi said.

The U.S. national debt exceeded $40 trillion for the first time on Tuesday, according to data released Wednesday by the Treasury Department. The alarming milestone comes less than a decade after the national debt first hit $20 trillion.

An Air Force major who was arrested last month after calling for the president’s impeachment was detained again for “pretrial confinement.” The man’s attorney said the legal team is awaiting the government’s evidence ahead of a detention hearing today.

Prince Harry, Meghan Markle and their two children are moving back to Britain in the coming weeks, according to multiple reports . The return of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex comes six years after they moved to the U.S. amid a clash with members of the royal family.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) heads to a closed-door Republican policy meeting at the Capitol in Washington, June 16, 2026. (J. Scott Applewhite, Associated Press)

‘ALMOST DISQUALIFYING’ : A key senator is already casting doubt on President Trump ’s nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) said in a post on social platform X that he has “strong concerns” about the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton , a top White House domestic policy adviser on health issues, which was announced on Wednesday. The senator said he respects Overton’s experience as a physician, but her lack of management experience doesn’t prepare her to lead a large agency “already dealing with staffing and morale issues.”

“Additionally, Dr. Overton’s active role in last week’s nonsensical vaccine executive order calls into question her commitment to standing up for sound science and protecting children’s health,” Cassidy said, referencing Trump’s executive order to push to reduce the childhood vaccine schedule and split up the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three separate shots.

Overton stood beside the president as he announced the order.

“That alone is almost disqualifying,” Cassidy, who is also a physician, said.

Trump chose Overton to lead the FDA as it’s dealt with an exodus of staff and a credibility crisis in the eyes of many in the healthcare industry. If confirmed, she would succeed Martin Makary , who resigned in May .

Cassidy’s opposition alone could be enough to sink the nomination, as he chairs the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee.

THIS IS FINE : Trump downplayed concerns about the U.S. bond market on Wednesday, even as the Treasury Department took extraordinary measures to reverse rising long-term bond yields.

The 30-year Treasury bond yield surpassed 5.3 percent on Tuesday, the highest mark recorded since 2007. That’s continued a trend of increases that’s taken place since the start of the Iran war.

Increasing bond yields push up mortgage rates and lead to higher borrowing costs for other products.

The spike prompted the Treasury to announce Wednesday that it will increase the maximum amount of U.S. debt that it can buy back. Starting next month, the maximum value of longer-dated securities that the Treasury can repurchase will double from $2 billion to $4 billion per operation.

Trump said he doesn’t believe Americans should be concerned about the volatility of the bond market. He reiterated his call for the Federal Reserve to reduce interest rates, calling them “artificially high.”

“They raise them for no reason, and you can’t go out to the market when you have a Fed that’s raising interest rates,” he said.

But the agency has continued to show hesitancy to lower rates, with many Fed officials indicating at a meeting late last month that interest rate hikes may be necessary.

CUT IN HALF : The Pentagon and South Korean military confirmed Wednesday that joint exercises between them will end almost a week early following Trump’s order reducing them.

Ulchi Freedom Shield began Monday and was scheduled to continue through Aug. 27 but will now end Aug. 21, a Defense Department official told The Hill. They said the U.S. military is continuing training that “enhances tactical capability,” but live-training events have been reduced, and some events have been canceled or converted to simulations.

Trump directed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to scale down the exercise, which takes place annually, just before they started, arguing they were hostile to North Korea. He also said he made the decision over his frustration with South Korea for not assisting in the U.S. war against Iran.

Trump has also said he’s in talks with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un to resume their diplomacy from his first term. However, Kim Yo Jong , a top adviser and Kim’s sister, denied knowledge of any such discussions in a message shared by state media.

South Korean officials have expressed concern about what this could mean for the future of the U.S.-South Korean alliance, which has been in place for decades and is meant to fend off North Korean aggression.

ETHICS PROBE : A woman accusing Rep. Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.) of misconduct told the House Ethics Committee on Wednesday that he sexually harassed and assaulted her.

Two attorneys for the woman said she was interviewed and told committee members that Gomez’s actions were not “consensual in nature,” contrary to a statement from the lawmaker that they were. Gomez told The Hill in a statement that he hasn’t violated any law or House Ethics rule.

“This is just the latest example of brazen sexual misconduct by a member of Congress,” the attorneys said. “Congress must act to rein in its members who seem to believe that preying on young women working on Capitol Hill is one of the perks of their job.”

The committee was first reported by CNN to be investigating Gomez in June following a New York Post story that he was allegedly seen kissing a younger staffer who worked for a different House Democrat in 2023. The panel confirmed on Monday that it is investigating the California Democrat.

Gomez has said he would cooperate with the investigation.

A nurse loads a syringe with a vaccine at an inoculation station in Jackson, Miss., Nov. 18, 2022. (Rogelio V. Solis, Associated Press file)

BREAKTHROUGH : An experimental personalized mRNA-based cancer vaccine was successful at preventing melanoma from returning or spreading in a late-stage trial of high-risk patients, potentially bringing a life-extending treatment closer to the market.

Merck and Moderna announced the development Wednesday, having combined the personalized vaccine Intismeran with Merck’s Keytruda in patients who had melanomas surgically removed.

The companies said the study met the main goal of extending “recurrence-free survival,” how long high-risk patients can live without their cancer coming back, and a secondary goal of preventing cancer from spreading to other parts of the body.

Intismeran is a personalized therapeutic designed to train and activate an antitumor response based on the unique mutational identity of a patient’s tumor. It’s developed using a tumor sample to identify the signature of their cancer and generate an immune response.

The mutations are encoded in mRNA and manufactured into a vaccine.

Melanoma accounts for only 1 percent of skin cancers but causes the highest percentage of deaths. Most cancer recurrences develop in the first two to three years after treatment, but melanoma can recur 10 or more years after it was first treated.

Merck Research Laboratories President Dean Li told CNBC’s “Squawk Box” that the companies will likely start talking to federal regulators in the next few months.

If the vaccine is approved, it would mark a major endorsement of Moderna’s mRNA platform.

MRNA was key in the COVID-19 vaccines that rolled out during the pandemic, and the technology has been viewed by many scientists as having significant potential toward treating other illnesses.

But it has faced political headwinds during the Trump administration, as Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and other officials have been sharply critical of the technology. Kennedy canceled hundreds of millions of dollars in mRNA vaccine funding last year, raising concerns among public health experts.

Still, the FDA did approve Moderna’s application last week for the first-ever mRNA flu vaccine, despite initial setbacks.

BIG BACKLASH : The Trump administration’s effort to construct a border wall through the Big Bend National Park in southwest Texas is encountering significant resistance from locals, ranging from environmental activists to county sheriffs.

Earlier this week, Customs and Border Protection (CBP) Commissioner Rodney Scott paused construction on the barriers until he “can get down there and do a personal evaluation,” amid pushback on the ground.

The Hill’s Rachel Frazin spoke to locals who are part of what Susan Hays , a lawyer who is running as a Democrat for Presidio County commissioner, called “a very organic grassroots movement” to oppose the construction.

“Our livelihoods are threatened at this point. Not just landowners, but business owners, and not just Big Bend National Park. … It’s everyone in this region,” said Yolanda Alvarado , a local cattle rancher and regional director for advocacy group No Big Bend Wall, whose property has been in her family for five generations.

“We are in line to lose a lot in our communities,” Alvarado said. “You can’t walk a mile without seeing a ‘no wall’ poster or bumper sticker. People are ready to fight back and stand up for their land.”

Outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn (R) recently wrote a letter urging federal officials to meet with stakeholders about the issue. And in March, bipartisan sheriffs from five counties wrote a letter opposing the wall.

CBP has shifted its plans for Big Bend National Park away from the wall, opting instead for an access road lined with vehicle barriers and new detection technology. But locals were not assuaged, saying the park’s remote location and rugged terrain already make illegal border crossings difficult.

“There’s not a piece of that portion of the border where you can actually drive a vehicle across the river. We have what I like to call the God-made barriers of the Rio Grande, the cliffs, the canyons that separate us, that make it impossible,” Terrell County Sheriff Thaddeus Cleveland , a Republican and former Border Patrol agent, told Frazin.

articles.title: What is Trump afraid we will see about how the tariffs were formulated?
articles.summary: When the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative unveiled its now-infamous “Liberation Day” tariff formula in April 2025, economists quickly noticed that something was not right. At first glance, the formula looked impressive. It had Greek symbols, academic citations, and all the trappings of serious economic analysis. But once economists began examining it, the sophistication quickly fell…
articles.body:
When the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative unveiled its now-infamous “Liberation Day” tariff formula in April 2025, economists quickly noticed that something was not right.

At first glance, the formula looked impressive. It had Greek symbols, academic citations, and all the trappings of serious economic analysis. But once economists began examining it, the sophistication quickly fell away. Key terms, they noticed, effectively cancel one another out, leaving little more than a calculation driven by bilateral trade deficits.

For one of us, an economist, that raised a simple question: How did this formula come to be? So he filed a Freedom of Information Act request seeking the records behind it. Then came more than a year of delays, missed deadlines, and back-and-forth with the U.S. Trade Representative.

When the agency finally responded, it said it had found 31 pages of responsive records. It would release none of them — not one email, calculation or even redacted paragraph. Rather, the office insisted that every page is protected because the records include communications between the agency and the White House Council of Economic Advisers about the reciprocal tariff calculations.

Whether those privileges ultimately apply is a question for the courts. But they do not answer the larger question. From an economist’s perspective, the response raises an obvious question: If the economic case for these tariffs was so strong, why is the government so determined to hide its work? And why wouldn’t the Council of Economic Advisers, a body of academic experts, put its name on a document that it reportedly helped to prepare?

For the other of us, the FOIA response raised a different, but closely related, concern. For two years, the Liberty Justice Center has represented businesses challenging the administration’s tariff actions in federal court. From that vantage point, these 31 hidden pages do not look like an isolated records dispute — they look like another piece of a much larger pattern.

Again and again, the legal justification has changed, even as the tariff policy has not. It was first justified under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. The administration argued that a statute intended for extraordinary national emergencies gave the president authority to impose sweeping tariffs around the world. When the courts rejected that theory, the White House cited Section 122, a temporary trade law that Congress had expressly limited to 150 days. When that authority was challenged — and then expired — the administration moved on to another statute.

Now it has turned to Section 301, using a sweeping forced-labor investigation involving dozens of countries to impose another broad tariff program. Different statutes, different legal theories and different public explanations always seem to lead back to remarkably similar tariffs.

The issue is no longer simply whether the administration chose the right tariff policy. It is whether the administration has been searching for new legal and economic justifications to preserve the same tariff policy after earlier justifications were rejected or expired. Viewed individually, each shift can perhaps be explained. Viewed together, they tell a very different story.

That question is now before the courts. But the denial of the Freedom of Information Act request raises the same concern from a different direction. Were law and the economics driving the policy? Or were the law and the economics being assembled to defend a policy that had already been chosen?

It also matters who was involved. The Council of Economic Advisers is supposed to provide the president with rigorous, objective economic analysis, and the U.S. Trade Representative’s response confirms that the council participated in discussions surrounding the tariff calculations.

If professional economists inside the council warned that the formula made little sense, the public deserves to know. If they endorsed it, the public deserves to know that, too. What should not happen is for the entire record to disappear behind a blanket claim of executive privilege.

The administration’s handling of one of its own academic sources only deepens the mystery. One of the main academic sources cited in support of the formula was a then-obscure working paper by economists Pau Pujolas and Jack Rossbach. Just days later, a link to the same paper appeared again in a speech by then-chairman Stephen Miran, defending the “Liberation Day” tariffs.

But one of the paper’s authors later said the administration had misused their research to support the opposite of what the paper actually found. As Pujolas explained, “there’s a huge gap between my study and what they’re doing.”

In other words, the administration cited academic research to support a tariff policy that one of the paper’s own authors publicly opposed. That episode shows that at least one of the administration’s academic citations was not merely debatable — it was publicly challenged by the scholars whose work was being cited.

The 31 withheld pages may reveal whether anyone inside the government recognized that problem before the formula was published, whether concerns were raised and ignored, or whether no one raised the alarm at all. And by withholding every page, the government has ensured that we cannot know.

Reasonable people disagree about tariffs, trade deficits, and industrial policy. But the executive branch owes the public an honest explanation for policies that affect hundreds of billions of dollars in commerce.

When the government asks courts to defer to its judgment, businesses to trust its reasoning, and the public to accept sweeping economic policies, it should be willing to show its work. What is this administration afraid we will see?

Phillip W. Magness is the David J. Theroux Chair in Political Economy at the Independent Institute. Sara Albrecht is chairman and CEO of the Liberty Justice Center, which represents businesses challenging the administration’s tariff actions.

articles.body:
Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom and U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle . Democratic strategist James Carville and GOP consultant Mary Matalin . Former GOP California Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger and Kennedy scion Maria Shriver .

These are just a few famous examples of some of the most prominent and well-known — past and present — bipartisan relationships in American politics — a phenomenon that some researchers believe make up as much as a quarter of U.S. romantic relationships.

Dating across partisan lines is no easy feat, particularly in an increasingly polarized political era. A working paper released earlier this month by two researchers at University of California, Berkeley’s Goldman School of Public Policy suggests that bipartisan couples or “politically mismatched” pairs are 14 percent less likely to remain together between election cycles compared to those who are in “politically matched” relationships

Yet, some cross-partisan couples are still a testament to the age-old idiom that opposites do, in fact, attract.

“The best way to navigate them is to avoid them, and we’ve been pretty good at that,” Carville told The Hill when asked about how to best navigate political differences.

Bipartisan couples few and far between, research says

It may not come as a surprise that most couples share the same political party affiliation or similar ideology.

A 2025 study conducted by researchers at the University of Michigan and University of California, Berkeley around politics and romantic relationships found that just 23 percent of couples surveyed had different political party affiliations. The working paper from earlier this month by Rachel Funk Fordham and Ernesto Tiburcio found similar results: 26 percent of the couples surveyed were politically “mismatched.”

Researchers have also found a higher correlation between political party support between couples compared to other factors.

A group of American and Australian professors published research in 2011 , for example, using survey data from the mid-1980s found that church attendance, political party support and drinking habits were the areas where couples were more likely to match compared to education, smoking frequency or weight.

So how do the ones that stay together make it work? For some, like Carville, it’s spending less time talking about politics.

“It’s more, I think, the mechanics and the maneuverings of politics that we engage on and less so the issues,” Democratic strategist Kevin Walling , who’s married to Republican strategist Alex Stroman , told The Hill.

“The only real night that — and again we’ve been together four or five years — we had a whole knockdown drag out fight over Harry Reid and Mitt Romney,” Walling added, referring to the former senators.

But other couples aren’t shy about delving into the issues, even if they don’t agree.

“If we have political discussions that get heated between us … we just agree to disagree, and we don’t take things personally,” Arash Mosaleh , a senior producer at Fox News’s “Gutfield!” who’s married to Colorado Democratic strategist Ted Trimpa , told The Hill.

“You also have to be willing to go to bed sometimes still mad,” Trimpa quipped.

Bipartisan couples, too, say there’s a lot to be learned from one another, including outside the scope of politics.

“When Kevin does his broadcasting, I think most people realize that he is open to other beliefs — I joke that we are both Republican/Democrat [but] not angry about it,” Stroman texted The Hill. “We know that it is easier to bring people your way, or at least have them consider your perspective, is not by beating them over the head with why your way is right and theirs wrong, but showing your thoughts and hearts and conclusions but being open to theirs.”

(Still, Stroman maintained that Walling is “obviously politically misinformed” and that his presence greatly benefits his husband.)

For Stamford Mayor Caroline Simmons , (D) who’s married to Rodeo Cannabis Company CEO and former Connecticut state Sen. Art Linares (R), it’s learning to have empathy for why people feel the way they do.

Learning about Linares’ family’s history escaping Cuba under communism “has helped informed me as to why he is Republican and kind of leans more conservative, more skeptical of big government and overregulation,” Simmons said.

Florida voters this week delivered a major upset in the Democratic primary for Senate, nominating a democratic socialist over the moderate frontrunner.

State Rep. Angie Nixon , a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), overcame a stark fundraising disadvantage to defeat Alex Vindman, a retired Army officer who served as a witness in President Trump’ s 2019 impeachment hearings. She’ll face off against Republican Sen. Ashley Moody for red seat this fall.

“Vindman was considered the favorite by almost everybody who watched the race,” said Aubrey Jewett , a political science professor at the University of Central Florida, pointing to Vindman’s national profile, anti-Trump posture and his “enormous” fundraising haul.

Vindman had pulled in more than $16 million, as of summer campaign finance filings, while Nixon hadn’t yet hit the $1 million mark. But the centrist’s fundraising edge failed to pay off on Election Day — and Nixon won the Democratic nod by roughly 12 points.

“The victory by Angie Nixon was the big deal in Florida, and I think emblematic of what we have seen in many states and local jurisdictions around the country, with the progressive wing of the Democratic Party, the socialist Democratic wing of the Democratic Party, really in ascendance.”

Nixon’s victory is the latest in a wave of progressive wins across the country this cycle, and her race against Vindman offered another test for the direction of a divided Democratic party — this time for a red seat far from the urban, blue enclaves where DSA candidates and other progressives have prevailed.

Nixon reportedly joined the DSA recently, but she didn’t lean heavily into the label along the campaign trail, and the national DSA organization did not back her bid.

“Maybe the label is not quite as important, but it still I think demonstrates that that progressive wing of the party is really at least in many states, including in Florida, this is the kind of candidate they’re looking for, and it makes up a strong majority of the party,” Jewett said.

As she pitched her progressive brand in the Senate race, Nixon brought a ground game that stood out to Democratic observers.

“Vindman raised a bunch of money, but he spent most of it raising money … It was an exceptionally low communication, low information primary,” said Florida Democratic strategist Steve Schale.

Schale shrugged off the framing of the race as a win for the DSA or a defeat for the establishment, arguing it came down to the candidates’ effort in the primary. He also suggested that Vindman, while a popular figure in Washington circles, was not as well-known in the Sunshine State.

Vindman, for his part, praised Nixon’s “strong campaign” in a post after the race was called, pledging to stand by her in the fight against Moody this fall.

Nixon’s progressive win, though, does appear to make the statewide race more difficult for her party in the red stronghold. Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved its rating of the Senate race toward Republicans after the primary, into “safe” red territory.

That raises new questions for Democrats about how to invest throughout Florida as the November election approaches.

“Does she have a chance? I still think the answer is yes, she has a chance, but it would be a big upset,” Jewett said.

Schale argued “the math is hard” for a Democratic win against Moody in President Trump’s home state. But he cautioned that the party shouldn’t write off Florida entirely.

“I worry if Democrats don’t think the top of the ticket’s worth investing in, it makes it a lot harder for those folks running down the ballot to have kind of the baseline they need to win,” he said.

articles.summary: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) doubled down Wednesday on his criticism of President Trump’s relationship with longtime White House aide Natalie Harp, brushing off a wave of attacks from the president’s inner circle over his remarks. Ossoff, who is seeking reelection in Georgia against Trump-backed Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), came under fire by the White House…
articles.body:
Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) doubled down Wednesday on his criticism of President Trump’s relationship with longtime White House aide Natalie Harp, brushing off a wave of attacks from the president’s inner circle over his remarks.

Ossoff, who is seeking reelection in Georgia against Trump-backed Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), came under fire by the White House during a campaign rally last weekend, where he brought up Harp in his critique of Trump.

“He golfs and trades stocks. See, he doesn’t want to do the job; he wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie to their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar,” Ossoff said, referring to the new Air Force One jet and pricey White House ballroom project .

Multiple people close to the president and Harp, who serves as his executive assistant, came to their defense, including the president’s son Eric Trump. The younger Trump called Ossoff’s comments “ absolute trash ” while White House communications director Steven Cheung launched vulgar attacks against the Georgia Democrat.

“It’s been amazing to watch this White House melt down over this all week,” Ossoff responded to the backlash during an interview with MS NOW.

He further waved off the scrutiny on Wednesday, saying Harp and other White House officials hold powerful government positions and should therefore be permissible targets of political criticism.

“These White House staffers are adults, public officials paid by the taxpayer with immense power in positions of public trust,” Ossoff told MS NOW’s Lawrence O’Donnell.

The senator also accused the aide of “printing out Donald Trump’s daily dose of delusion and flattery” and lambasted comments made by White House trade adviser Peter Navarro and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

“No one cares about their feelings,” Ossoff said.

Harp has drawn increased attention in recent days over her close relationship with the president. The New York Times reported that Harp frequently accompanies President Trump on his golf trips and to his Mar-a-Lago resort, helps draft his posts on social media and carries a portable printer to provide him information in hard copy.

Her estranged brother, Preston Harp, described her devotion to Trump as an “unhealthy obsession” in an interview with CNN.

Eric Trump, in response, maintained that Harp is “an incredible young woman” and “arguably one of the hardest-working people in the White House.”

articles.title: Mark your calendars — Democrats are ready for 2028
articles.summary: The Democratic Party belongs to all Democrats. It belongs to every wing of our party, every region of our country, and people from every walk of life. It belongs to those who live in major cities, rural communities, suburbs and small towns. It belongs to those who have been active in our party for decades and those…
articles.body:
The Democratic Party belongs to all Democrats. It belongs to every wing of our party, every region of our country, and people from every walk of life. It belongs to those who live in major cities, rural communities, suburbs and small towns. It belongs to those who have been active in our party for decades and those casting their first-ever primary ballot.

Our primary calendar for the next presidential election reflects just that.

As co-chairs of the Democratic National Committee’s Rules and Bylaws Committee, responsible for fairly reflecting the scope of America in the 2028 primary, we believe the best decisions are made when everyone has a seat at the table, debates are held out in the open, and the process earns the trust of everyone involved.

Over the weekend, Democrats delivered on that promise by officially approving six “early window” states for our 2028 presidential nominating calendar: South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia.

This proposed lineup is the result of 10 months of hard work, numerous open meetings, and dozens of hours of public deliberation. It also makes history — for the first time in decades, we have a new early-window calendar with a wide-open field.

Most importantly for our party, this calendar puts Democrats in the best position possible to win back the White House in 2028. It rigorously tests our candidates across key battleground states and an increasingly diverse electorate, while keeping the contest open and affordable so that voters, not money, decide our nominee.

That nominee, whoever it is, will have to appeal to a wide range of voters. The calendar the DNC passed demands that candidates not only introduce themselves but prove themselves to every type of voter, including those who will be key to winning the general election.

That is why our early window puts four battleground states — Nevada, New Hampshire, Michigan and Virginia — at the start of our nominating contest, while also including states with competitive down-ballot races and swing-voter populations, like South Carolina and New Mexico.

At the same time, our calendar amplifies the voices of Black voters, who are a foundation of the Democratic Party. This is especially important in the wake of the Louisiana v. Callais ruling, which has allowed Republicans to racially gerrymander the electoral map . Black voters have carried our party through its most consequential elections in the past, yet Republicans across the country are seeking to remove Black voices from the halls of government.

In 2028, the Democratic Party is putting those voices front and center to help shape the future of our country. With an eye toward growing regions of the country and where political power will reorient after the next census, this early window further recognizes the growing importance of the South and Sun Belt regions that are poised to gain additional representation in years to come.

Finally, this early-window calendar is efficient, not only for the states holding the contests but for the candidates competing in them. All six of these states have a proven track record of running fair, transparent and inclusive contests. Whether they are geographically compact, like New Hampshire, have affordable media markets, like Nevada, or feature both, like South Carolina, this early window doesn’t box out any candidates. Our presidential nominating process shouldn’t be restricted to those who have the biggest bank account, the highest name recognition, or the greatest head start. Rather, it should allow all candidates to introduce themselves to voters without being priced out before the process has truly begun.

This calendar, and the process used to put it together, accomplishes that. Because of reforms proposed by DNC Chair Ken Martin, the Rules and Bylaws Committee was expanded to its largest membership in history. For the first time ever, committee members were chosen directly by the DNC’s caucuses and councils, ensuring that voices from all across our party and country had a say in determining our calendar. Because this was the most representative Rules and Bylaws Committee in our history, it produced the most diverse early-state calendar in our history.

We are proud that the calendar has earned support and praise from a broad range of Democrats, elected officials and advocates alike who recognize the strength of the early window. It battle-tests our candidates, represents the full array of voters and establishes a fair, open and affordable process for anyone seeking the nomination.

That is what happens when we open the doors, broaden participation and trust the full diversity of our party to help lead. Better decisions are made when more voices are included, and if Democrats are going to defend democracy throughout our country, then we must be wholly committed to practicing it inside our party, too.

At the end of the day, this calendar strengthens our party by welcoming in millions of Americans. Because of the work that we’ve accomplished, our eventual nominee will enter the general election in the best position to unite our coalition and to compete in every part of the country. And when — not if — we flip the White House in 2028, it will be because of the work that our committee, and so many Democrats across the country, are doing to ensure we get there.

Minyon Moore and Jim Roosevelt are co-chairs of the Democratic National Committee’s Rules and Bylaws Committee.

articles.title: Presidents sometimes defy Congress and the courts with executive orders
articles.summary: President Donald Trump has significantly increased the use of executive orders during his second term, challenging previous records for judicial pushback while navigating a period of legislative scarcity.
articles.body:
As much as presidents complain about the other two branches usurping their constitutional prerogatives as chief executive, they can, at times, also trample the turf of the other branches.

Last week, the Washington Post carried an article on the various ways President Trump has used executive orders to circumvent or defy the courts or Congress. The three examples cited were on high court rulings against Trump’s tariffs, birthright citizenship and the dismissal of a Federal Reserve Board governor. In each instance, the president has subsequently devised alternative approaches to exploit perceived loopholes in the court’s rulings. This is not something Trump did in his first term as president, but second terms seem to invite last chance gambits in which losing does not carry the same consequences.

The Post cited its own analysis in which the president and his appointees have been accused of flouting court rulings in more than 160 lawsuits against the administration.

The Founders might have been appalled at the extent to which the executive branch has come out on top in so many of these conflicts since they thought the Congress would pose a greater threat of dominance. But presidents learned early how to play the game harder and more stealthily, sometimes going to extremes to test (or stretch) boundaries.

Where did the whole notion of presidential executive orders originate, and what are they, exactly? Perhaps not surprisingly, our first president, George Washington, issued the first executive order on June 8, 1789 , in which he directed the heads of all executive departments to “impress [him] with a full, precise and distinct general idea of the affairs of the United States” in their particular fields of jurisdiction. In his two terms as president, though, Washington only issued eight executive orders.

Executive orders have no explicit statutory grounding or required format. They are simply recognized as one of the implied powers of the president to direct how the government is to be managed and operated. They can only be issued by the president and only be binding on the executive branch. They can range from instructions on how to enforce a law or how to manage executive branch employees and resources. Executive orders can be subject to review by the courts and overturned if they are not grounded in the Constitution or in statute. Once issued, the orders remain in force until they are canceled, adjudicated as unlawful, or expire under their own terms.

Not surprisingly, the number of executive orders issued by presidents grew considerably over the years as the number of laws increased along with the size and scope of government. Abraham Lincoln issued 48 executive orders , the most famous of which was the Emancipation Proclamation, initially on Sept. 22, 1862. It changed the legal status of more than 3.5 million enslaved African Americans in those Confederate states already under control of the Union army.

Lincoln did run afoul of the Supreme Court when he suspended habeas corpus in 1861without congressional authorization . Chief Justice Roger Taney, writing for the majority in Ex parte Merryman, held that Lincoln’s actions were unconstitutional since only the Congress has that authority under Article I, section 9.

Beginning with the progressive era, the number of executive orders escalated: Teddy Roosevelt issued 1,081; Woodrow Wilson, 1,803; and Franklin Roosevelt, 3,721. But the Supreme Court pushed back on Roosevelt, holding five of his orders unconstitutional in 1935 alone.

Perhaps not surprisingly President Lyndon Johnson (1963-1969) issued only 325 executive orders. That is because he was able to enact most of his Great Society programs as laws through an overwhelmingly Democratic Congress in his early years as president.

President Trump issued 220 executive orders in his first term. But, after a four-year hiatus under President Joe Biden (162 executive orders), Trump came back and issued 275 orders in the first 100 days of his second term.

Having run against Biden’s use of autopens, the president was more than happy to pose frequently wielding his Sharpies to sign bills and executive orders. In his first and second terms to date, Trump issued 495 orders, the ninth most of any president in history. Most of his second term orders have dealt with foreign policy issues.

With the paucity of new laws being enacted by Congress in the last few years, it is perhaps understandable that a president would look to other means to accomplish his policy goals. Trump has dared to challenge Roosevelt’s record for Supreme Court setbacks over executive orders, and is well on his way to exceeding it.

Don Wolfensberger is a 28-year congressional staff veteran, culminating as chief of staff of the House Rules Committee. He is author of “Congress and the People: Deliberative Democracy on Trial” (2000), and, “Changing Cultures in Congress: From Fair Play to Power Plays” (2028).

articles.title: Darline Graham on debate question stumble: ‘I’m not a politician’
articles.summary: Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) on Wednesday defended her stumble earlier this week on a national security question during a primary runoff debate, saying she was simply being “honest” about her lack of political experience. “I tripped up on one question last night regarding Taiwan,” Graham said in an interview with Fox News on Wednesday. “I…
articles.body:
Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) on Wednesday defended her stumble earlier this week on a national security question during a primary runoff debate, saying she was simply being “honest” about her lack of political experience.

“I tripped up on one question last night regarding Taiwan,” Graham said in an interview with Fox News on Wednesday. “I have said many times I’m not a politician, certainly not a career politician. I don’t speak politician.”

Graham, who was appointed to fill the vacancy left after her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), died last month , was asked during the special GOP debate on Tuesday whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues for the U.S. and why.

“I’m just going to be honest here. I’m not that informed on national security,” she responded. “But I do support the military.”

By contrast, her late brother served in the Air Force for more than three decades and had extensive national security experience, including serving as a member on several top Senate committees focused on defense.

Former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley (R) ripped Darline Graham’s national security answer, arguing that her brother’s experience could not be passed on to her.

“Lindsey Graham was well informed on the United States’ national security. Darline Graham admits she’s not,” Haley wrote on social platform X . “This is not something you inherit. And it’s critical in the U.S. Senate.”

The senator’s debate answer drew boos from the audience and criticism as she competes for a full term in the Senate. President Trump recommended her to replace her brother and has endorsed her campaign.

Graham sought to clarify her position in Wednesday’s interview, adding that people across the state “appreciated” the fact that she was transparent about her knowledge.

“I did say several times that, you know, China is our enemy, our military and economic threat to the United States,” she said. “Of course, Taiwan is our friend.”

She argued, however, that her constituents are more focused on domestic concerns.

“I think people in South Carolina are more worried about making ends meet,” she said. “So, they are concerned about a lot of other things other than Taiwan.”

The runoff election between Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) is set for Tuesday.

articles.body:
White House legislative director James Braid is leaving his post, Vice President Vance announced on Thursday .

Braid’s departure comes ahead of November’s midterm elections and at a time when President Trump’s relationship with Senate Republicans has grown rocky . Additionally, Braid, who was previously Vance’s legislative director in the Senate, is departing as the vice president considers a presidential run in 2028.

“Not only is James brilliant, he is one of the hardest workers you will ever meet. He’s been with me in every fight I’ve been in, from day one in my senate office through the transition and the President’s transformative second term. He has served the President with distinction and I couldn’t be prouder of him,” Vance said in a post on the social platform X.

“Very excited to see what he does next,” the vice president added.

Braid’s departure comes as Republicans face an uphill battle in retaining their majorities in the House and the Senate.

Braid played a key role in ushering major pieces of Trump’s legislative agenda through Congress, including the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, as well as Trump’s Cabinet and judicial nominees.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) praised Braid for his “extraordinary skill” leading the White House Office of Legislative Affairs.

“His great friendship, unwavering commitment, and tireless work ethic have helped House and Senate Republicans advance President Trump’s America First agenda in spite of our razor-thin majorities, and he has played an essential role in delivering historic results for the American people,” Johnson wrote in a post on X on Thursday.

In addition to serving as a link between both ends of Pennsylvania Avenue, Braid was also a key link between Trump’s and Vance’s orbits going into the president’s second administration.

articles.title: Panama is one battle in China’s infrastructure war
articles.summary: China has retaliated against Panama by increasing inspections and detentions of Panamanian-flagged ships after the Panamanian Supreme Court struck down concessions held by a Hong Kong-based company at the entrance terminals of the Panama Canal.
articles.body:
Panama is paying a price for stepping away from Beijing. Recent reporting indicates that Chinese authorities have sharply increased inspections and detentions of Panamanian-flagged ships after Panama’s Supreme Court struck down the concessions held by Hong Kong-based CK Hutchison at the Balboa and Cristobal container terminals. Beijing says the measures are based on safety concerns. Panamanian officials see them as retaliation for a decision that weakened China’s commercial position at both ends of the Panama Canal.

Panama is one battle in a much larger contest over who will shape the Western Hemisphere. For more than two decades, China expanded its reach by financing, building, and operating ports, railways, electrical grids, telecommunications systems, logistics hubs, and energy projects across Latin America. Those investments created influence that extends well beyond commerce.

But Washington has begun pushing back. The dispute in Panama offers an early look at how difficult it may be to reverse two decades of Chinese infrastructure expansion.

My first assignment after joining the U.S. Army was in the Panama Canal Zone. While serving there, I came to appreciate the canal as much more than a waterway connecting the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. It remains one of the greatest engineering achievements in history and a lasting reminder of what American vision, resources and determination can accomplish.

Built under the direction of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers after overcoming disease, unforgiving terrain and immense technical challenges, the canal transformed global commerce while giving the United States an enduring strategic advantage in the Western Hemisphere.

One of us recently returned from Panama, where conversations repeatedly turned to China’s presence around the canal and across the country. Many Americans have only recently begun paying attention. Panamanians have watched this expansion unfold for years. The U.S. allowed its attention to drift while Chinese companies steadily pursued projects near one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints, less than four hours by air from Miami.

Panama recognized the People’s Republic of China in 2017 , ended diplomatic relations with Taiwan, and joined the Belt and Road Initiative the following year. Chinese firms pursued the proposed Panama City-David railway, the Fourth Bridge over the Panama Canal, the Amador Cruise Terminal, and other large projects.

The greatest concern centered on the Balboa and Cristobal terminals at the Pacific and Atlantic entrances to the canal, operated by Panama Ports Company, a subsidiary of CK Hutchison. China did not own or operate the canal, but companies tied to Beijing had gained influence over commercial infrastructure surrounding it.

Panama is not unique. China’s state-owned COSCO Shipping built and now operates the deep-water port at Chancay in Peru. State Grid of China invested heavily in Brazil’s electricity transmission network. Chinese firms expanded into energy, mining, transportation and telecommunications throughout the region. In Venezuela, more than $60 billion in Chinese lending helped secure access to oil while China supported the Maduro regime through years of isolation.

Each deal had its own commercial explanation, yet the larger result was a network of Chinese influence spread across ports, power systems, supply chains and national economies.

Washington increasingly viewed Chinese influence surrounding the canal as a national security concern. It elevated the issue in discussions with Panama, encouraged greater American investment, and supported efforts that led CK Hutchison to agree to sell its controlling interest in the terminals to a U.S.-led consortium.

Panama also withdrew from China’s Belt and Road Initiative . When Chinese opposition delayed the proposed sale, Panama’s Supreme Court struck down the port concessions, clearing the way for new management. Panama became the first visible effort to reverse a much broader Chinese strategy built on infrastructure throughout Latin America.

Beijing’s response illustrates why control of infrastructure matters. Ports move trade, electrical grids power economies, telecommunications systems carry information, and logistics hubs connect global supply chains. Once countries become dependent on those systems, commercial relationships can become political leverage. Panama’s shipping registry is now feeling that pressure through delays, inspections, and the possibility that shipowners will move their vessels elsewhere.

Panama will not be the last contest over Chinese infrastructure in the Western Hemisphere. Similar battles are likely wherever ports, railroads, electrical grids, telecommunications networks and logistics hubs intersect with national security.

China spent more than two decades building this position through investment, construction and long-term commercial relationships rather than military force. Reversing it will require the U.S. to compete with the same patience and persistence that allowed Beijing to build it in the first place.

John Spencer is the chair of war studies at the Madison Policy Forum, where Frank Viola is a fellow.

articles.title: Trump shows off White House construction projects: ‘We get the best stuff’
articles.summary: President Trump on Wednesday showed reporters a closer look at the White House’s various construction projects, including the ballroom and new helipad, saying “we get the best stuff.” Trump led an uninterrupted, 30-minute tour of the new White House helipad designed for Marine One, which, when completed, will be 100 feet wide, made of granite…
articles.body:
President Trump on Wednesday showed reporters a closer look at the White House’s various construction projects, including the ballroom and new helipad , saying “we get the best stuff.”

Trump led an uninterrupted, 30-minute tour of the new White House helipad designed for Marine One, which, when completed, will be 100 feet wide, made of granite and adorned with the presidential seal. Trump signed the underside of the slab while talking to reporters.

The president also praised the slab’s durability and said it will be “here for a long time.”

“We get the best stuff; one thing I know how to do is build,” he told reporters .

Trump heralded how the helipad will “look incredible from the air and from every place else” and highlighted that it will be used for celebratory events and meetings, including his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Workers told the president that the landing pad will be completed by Sept. 21, two days before Xi’s planned arrival.

“We might make it for President Xi,” Trump replied. “That’d be nice but not imperative.”

The granite used for the helipad measures at 4 inches thick and was dug out of a quarry in California, with “The Seal of the United States of America” carved into it, Reuters reported .

“This will be much better for state arrivals,” the president ​said. “And in fact, instead of being on grass, now they’ll be using that almost like a table. They can have events on it. They can have ​people go there for cocktails and then walk to the ballroom after that’s finished.”

He also emphasized the durability of the slab, saying it will “be here long after we’re gone, no matter what happens with the world, this is not moving. This will take any kind of shot.”

He requested earlier this month that construction crews tear up the helipad after he was frustrated with its appearance, according to The Washington Post . Two people familiar with the project told the outlet that the president had expressed interest in adding a landing pad level with the horizon, which would require disassembling the helipad and leveling the South Lawn.

“Nice job, fellas. Does anybody know the word ‘media’? This is serious media and you guys are doing a great job. Sorry to take an extra week and a half, but lifting it up was one of the best things we’ve ever done,” Trump told crews working on the helipad on Wednesday, confirming the Post’s reporting.

He celebrated the driveway leading up to the southern portico, as well, saying there were previously potholes in the roadway.

“It’s ridiculous the way this place was taken care of,” Trump continued. “Nobody, including other presidents, they didn’t see it. But I see it because I was very good at real estate, like maybe the best, in a lot of ways. I love construction. I love seeing things properly taken care of.”

The president also took notice of the two flagpoles on the northern and southern sides of the White House, which he donated to himself.

“This is a great pole,” Trump said. “This is a top-of-the-line — it’s tapered. This isn’t a straight up-and-down job, which looks terrible, frankly. It’s a tapered pole, great — I’m very good at flagpoles.”

The walls of the White House ballroom towered behind everyone as construction on the planned 90,000-square-foot addition to the executive mansion went on.

“We’ve gotten tremendous architectural reviews,” he said about the project. “It’s beautiful.”

The National Trust for Historic Preservation is challenging the project, arguing to the Supreme Court on Tuesday that the administration’s emergency request to allow construction must be denied. The Trump administration wants the justices to step in to stop a lower court order that would grind the above-ground work to a halt starting at the end of the day on Friday.

Trump characterized his effort to revamp the White House as long overdue

“This building was falling apart,” he told reporters. “It’s falling apart –– like buying a building in New York City that’s in bad shape ​and putting it back together. That’s what I used to do. I did it better than anybody, I think.”

articles.title: Reform UK proposes tax rebates for firms to boost apprenticeships
articles.summary: Suella Braverman also advised student's "not to get ripped off by the great university scam".
articles.body:
Young apprentices should have part of their wages paid by taxpayers, according to Reform UK plans , external aimed at delivering a "skills revolution".

The party's education spokeswoman Suella Braverman said a Reform government would introduce an "apprenticeship wage credit" offering small and medium-sized businesses a 30% rebate on the wages of apprentices they take on aged 16 to 18.

She also advised students receiving their GCSE exam results on Thursday "not to get ripped off by the great university scam" and to learn a trade instead.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he wants teenagers to have technical routes into careers that could rival the path of a traditional university degree.

The government has been introducing changes and examining ways to encourage more young people into work, including giving some parents on benefits up to Â£4,500 a year to encourage their children to start apprenticeships.

Former minister Alan Milburn has been tasked with investigating why so many young people are not in employment, education or training - known by the acronym Neets.

Reform said its announcement was the first in a series of proposals aimed at reaching 600,000 apprenticeship starts per year by the end of the next Parliament, likely to be 2034.

The party says it would pay for its plans by banning all foreign students from accessing taxpayer-funded loans and stopping what the party calls "Mickey Mouse degrees".

Reform said its policy, which also includes a Â£2,000 retention bonus for apprentices, could cost between Â£1.48bn and almost Â£2bn over five years.

Braverman said there are "excessive number of graduates with qualifications that don't match the skills needed for our country," arguing that learning a trade would be a better use of their time.

Apprentices are generally paid a lower wage but get on-the-job training and practical work experience.

Speaking at a press conference, Braverman said: "We're firing the starting gun on unleashing a technical and vocational renaissance of homegrown skills.

"Reform will not do this because it fills us with some jingoistic pride but because we will do what it takes to save Britain from the perpetual doom loop of decline, debt and despair that we're currently in."

The MP said the apprenticeship wage credit would result in businesses saving an average of Â£4,000-a-year per apprentice.

The Â£2,000 tax-free retention bonus would be paid to workers who "show loyalty" by staying with the business that trained them for at least two years after they complete their apprenticeship, said Braverman.

Asked if the policy would mean some universities would have to close, Braverman said she did not envisage that but instead suggested universities need to "repurpose" themselves into construction colleges and manufacturing colleges.

When pressed to give examples of "Mickey Mouse degrees", Braverman pointed to "gender studies" and "golf course studies".

She said: "There's not a necessity, there's not a value in many of these degrees."

The British and International Golf Greenkeepers Association (BIGGA) has previously criticised Braverman for similar remarks, which they branded "negligent and potentially damaging".

BIGGA chief executive Jim Croxton said: "Golf course management is a growing industry with currently more vacancies than qualified applicants.

"Anyone successfully studying for a degree in this field is effectively guaranteed employment in a vibrant industry."

A Labour Party spokesperson said all young people "deserve a clear route to a good career" whether through "a properly funded apprenticeship, high-quality technical education or university".

The spokesperson added: "That's exactly what this Labour government is already delivering, with 500,000 new jobs, apprenticeships and training opportunities to help young people earn or learn, including a guaranteed job for 18â24-year-olds who have been out of work for 18 months."

On Wednesday, Conservative shadow education secretary Laura Trott said there is demand for apprenticeships but claimed the Labour government "aren't doing enough to boost supply".

She said: "Our New Deal for Young People would axe the dead end degrees that don't lead to jobs and instead invest in apprenticeships giving school leavers more choice."

Liberal Democrat universities spokesperson Ian Sollom said it was important to protect local colleges and universities as well as boosting apprenticeships, including apprenticeships in degree courses.

"Reform's proposals amount to dangerous economic vandalism which would rip a multi-billion-pound hole in our world-leading university sector," he added.

Green Party MP Hannah Spencer, who was a plumber before becoming an MP, said: "People are tired of Reform pitting us against each other - Those of us that did apprenticeships can still see the value in degrees and everyone should be able to choose their own path of education."

She added the Greens had announced a windfall tax on big banks , which she said would support small businesses employing more young people.

articles.title: Alina Habba says she’s ‘not in the running’ to replace Leavitt

articles.body:
Alina Habba, the president’s former personal attorney, ruled herself out as a candidate for White House press secretary as speculation swirls about whom President Trump will pick to replace Karoline Leavitt.

“Flattered by the Kalshi odds, but I’m not in the running for any job,” Habba wrote in a social media post on Wednesday, referring to the popular prediction market. “However, if I’m getting a new one, I’d love for one of these anonymous sources to let me know first.”

Habba is one of several public figures and people close to the president who are believed to be on a shortlist of potential candidates to replace Leavitt, who is slated to leave the White House this month.

Leavitt, the only person to serve as Trump’s press secretary during his second term, announced earlier this month she was leaving the job to spend more time with her family.

The top spokesperson for Trump’s 2024 campaign, she recently had a second child.

Habba made a name for herself in the media defending Trump while he was out of office and faced various charges relating to his businesses, handling of classified documents and attempts to overturn the 2020 election.

“Fake news remains the undefeated champ,” Habba wrote in her social media post. “Well…until I come at them.”

articles.title: Trump can reduce hostility for immigration enforcement — without weakening it
articles.summary: There are changes Trump can make in enforcing his immigration to reduce hostilities and the number of legal challenges.
articles.body:
Border czar Tom Homan has had record-breaking success with his border security measures. Apprehensions at the Southwest border have declined to levels not seen in more than three decades. This is because, as the Department of Homeland Security claims, the border is more secure now than at any point in history .

The Trump administration has had success with interior enforcement, too, but its enforcement measures there have resulted in a lot of public hostility and a tsunami of lawsuits. But it doesn’t have to be this way. President Trump can implement his enforcement policies just as effectively, but with less hostility and fewer lawsuits, if he just adopts a few smart changes.

First, his administration should change its litigation strategy. The ACLU brought 434 legal actions against Trump during his first term in office, and 230 legal actions against him during just the first year of his second term. The best way to stop or weaken this campaign to block Trump’s immigration policies is to learn as much as possible about what the activist organization is doing and why.

A January ACLU report titled “ Defeat, Delay, Dilute: ACLU Versus President Trump ” explains the strategy. The administration also should study the ACLU’s successful lawsuits to learn how to make new enforcement initiatives less vulnerable to avoidable litigation.

A second tip pertains to the use of masks and badges. Homan says that ICE officers in the field need masks to protect them and their families from what has been called doxxing, or the malicious exposure of their personal information. It is a crime to make personal information about ICE officers available to the public, to to threaten or incite violence against officers and their families, who are just doing their jobs.

The strongest objection to face masks is that they reduce accountability. This is a legitimate concern, but ICE officers can be identified even if they are wearing masks. The agency can assign unique identification numbers to each officer and put those numbers and the names of the offices they work for on badges. Then simply require them to wear the badges when they are conducting field operations. This would substantially reduce the risk of doxxing, while the identities of the numbered officers could be made available to the ICE Office of Professional Responsibility , the Homeland Security inspector general , and congressional oversight committees as needed.

Third, the Executive Office for Immigration Review is using military lawyers as temporary immigration judges without requiring them to have direct immigration experience. This is intended to address a growing backlog of cases at the courts. But using judges inexperienced in immigration law unnecessarily increases the risk of reversible error and due process challenges. It would be better to use these lawyers primarily to preside over master calendar hearings until they have more experience.

As the office puts it, “Master calendar hearings are held for pleadings, scheduling, and other similar matters. It should be possible to train these newcomers for these responsibilities and to handle relatively straightforward in-absentia proceedings for aliens who fail to appear at the master calendar hearings despite receiving proper notification. This way, more experienced immigration judges can handle more complex matters.

ICE should also reexamine its priorities for detention. As of July 11, ICE was detaining 65,765 immigrants, but many of these might not need to be detained. The agency should give priority to detaining aliens who are subject to mandatory detention , which includes the 90-day “ removal period ” for aliens with a final removal order. When detention is discretionary, ICE generally should release aliens unless an individual assessment indicates that detention is necessary due to a public safety or flight risk. In questionable cases, ICE’s Alternatives to Detention program can be used to minimize the risk that aliens will abscond.

In May, the Department of Homeland Security shut down the Office of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman that provided independent oversight of immigration detention facilities because Congress had not provided funding for that office. Its responsibilities included handling complaints about conditions in detention facilities.

The department should ask Congress to restore funding for this office. In addition to helping immigrants subject to detention, it provides an independent mechanism for identifying and correcting problems before they become scandals or lawsuits.

According to a recent Economist-YouGov poll , 48 percent of Americans support abolishing ICE, and 40 percent oppose abolishing it. Moreover, 42 percent do not have any confidence in ICE, 11 percent have only a little, and only 22 percent have a great deal of confidence in the agency. Fifty-eight percent think ICE has used too much force; only 30 percent think its use of force has been necessary and justified.

ICE’s Office of Public Affairs is supposed to prevent such negative reactions to enforcement operations. It should redouble its efforts to bolster public confidence.

Better-trained judges, unique numbers for identifying masked officers without exposing them, the elimination of unnecessary detentions, the restoration of an independent detention-complaint office and greater transparency would all make enforcement measures more defensible legally and politically, without reducing their effectiveness.

Nolan Rappaport was detailed to the House Judiciary Committee as an executive branch immigration law expert for three years. He subsequently served as an immigration counsel for the Subcommittee on Immigration, Border Security and Claims for four years. Prior to working on the Judiciary Committee, he wrote decisions for the Board of Immigration Appeals for 20 years.
