articles.title: Scavino warns officials fired for doing ‘s‑‑‑ty job’ against media attacks
articles.summary: White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino tore into unnamed former staffers in a profanity-laced post on social media, telling those who had been fired or passed over for jobs to stop bashing the administration in the media and “take the L.” “When you get fired for doing a spectacularly s—ty job at an…
articles.body:
White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino tore into unnamed former staffers in a profanity-laced post on social media, telling those who had been fired or passed over for jobs to stop bashing the administration in the media and “take the L.”

“When you get fired for doing a spectacularly s—ty job at an agency, with your badge deactivated, building access revoked, and the full ‘you’re dead to us’ package — or when you get passed over for Ambassadorships, Boards, or Commissions — because there are candidates who are actually far more qualified than you, please resist the urge to sprint to every media outlet that will platform your lying bull s—, and then falsely attack the people in the Presidential Personnel Office who are out here serving President Trump, the Administration, and the American people each and every day,” Scavino wrote on the social platform X .

“Just take the L, and move on, LOSER,” he added.

Scavino, one of President Trump’s longest-serving aides, did not say whom the late Wednesday post was directed toward, though several prominent figures have been fired or left their posts throughout Trump’s second term.

FBI Director Kash Patel backed the rant , writing from his personal X account, “Boss Move, Dan’s a legend.”

Several Trump allies also pondered whom the aide may have been referencing in his post.

Far-right influencer and Trump loyalist Laura Loomer wrote on X : “Wonder who he is talking about.” White House principal deputy communications director Kaelan Dorr also threw his support behind the rant in a series of emojis .

Scavino has led the Presidential Personnel Office since last year while continuing to serve as White House deputy chief of staff. His office oversees the selection and vetting of thousands of political appointees across the federal government.

His critique comes as tensions over potential leaks and public criticisms from inside Trump’s orbit have spilled into the media in recent weeks. The White House has also brushed off waves of scrutiny surrounding the close relationship between Trump and his executive assistant Natalie Harp.

articles.title: O’Reilly: Trump endorsement ‘doesn’t have the cachet that it did’ because of Iran
articles.summary: Political commentator Bill O’Reilly on Wednesday said an endorsement from President Trump “doesn’t have the cachet that it did” previously, citing the Iran war. O’Reilly and NewsNation’s Chris Cuomo talked about Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), who secured the Republican nomination in Florida’s gubernatorial race. Trump has endorsed Donalds, but the candidate said it is the…
articles.body:
Political commentator Bill O’Reilly on Wednesday said an endorsement from President Trump “doesn’t have the cachet that it did” previously, citing the Iran war.

O’Reilly and NewsNation’s Chris Cuomo talked about Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), who secured the Republican nomination in Florida’s gubernatorial race. Trump has endorsed Donalds, but the candidate said it is the president’s decision regarding whether to hit the campaign trail with the Florida lawmaker.

“I don’t know if that means anything now, because Donald Trump has got to solve the Iran thing,” O’Reilly said during his “Cuomo” appearance. “That is really hurting him. Because then the prices follow that. They’re haunting him. So I don’t know if the endorsement –– it’s not going to hurt you if you’re a Republican. No, but it doesn’t have the cachet that it did.”

O’Reilly predicted that Donalds will win the November election and succeed Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R), “but it’ll be close” unless Donalds can “shake” Florida Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly in a debate.

Cuomo then pressed the former Fox News host on Trump’s handling of the Iran war, its impact on the economy and its unpopularity among Americans, and if Trump can “save your party from having to own your mistake?”

“Listen, I don’t get the daily briefings,” O’Reilly replied. “I don’t know what the intel is. All I know is that this is tied into President Trump’s legacy now. This is personal, as they said in ‘The Godfather’: ‘It’s business, not personal, Sonny,’ OK? So he’s got to come out as the winner in Iran somehow.”

O’Reilly said there is “no doubt” Trump will not sell taking over Iran’s Kharg Island, which holds around 90 percent of Iran’s crude oil exports. Cuomo said that selling the war “is the big problem he has.”

O’Reilly said he was “not sure about that,” emphasizing the Trump administration’s claim that preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon prompted the conflict.

Republican lawmakers have largely stood behind Trump in his military action against Iran, but some have expressed that it could be a political liability come November. Democrats have used the conflict as part of their messaging on the campaign trail.

Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.), whose term ends in January, recently warned that the Iran conflict could be the U.S.’s “ next forever war .”

“And I think it is with gas prices rising again and our oil reserves going down, this is, you know, problematic for a lot of reasons because … the Iran conflict is not on the ballot in November, but affordability is, and the cost of living is, and this thing has increased our cost of living,” she said.

The Iran war could also depress Republican turnout ahead of the midterms, according to polling taken by Politico in July.

Retiring Rep. Michael McCaul (R-Texas) told CNN at the time that the U.S. should negotiate “from the rubble.”

“I think this back-and-forth approach is not the right one, and it will guarantee that this thing delays into the midterm elections, which is precisely what Iran is trying to do right now,” he said.

articles.title: Ocasio-Cortez backs Markey in Massachusetts Senate primary
articles.summary: Democratic Sen. Ed Markey (Mass.) received a boost to his reelection bid Thursday with an endorsement from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.). Markey is engaged in a competitive Democratic primary race against Rep. Seth Moulton (D-Mass.). The two candidates have sought to build upon a growing antiestablishment sentiment in the Democratic Party in their campaigns. Moulton…
articles.body:
Democratic Sen. Ed Markey (Mass.) received a boost to his reelection bid Thursday with an endorsement from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.).

Markey is engaged in a competitive Democratic primary race against Rep. Seth Moulton (D-Mass.). The two candidates have sought to build upon a growing antiestablishment sentiment in the Democratic Party in their campaigns.

Moulton has said it is time for generational change in his bid to replace the 80-year-old incumbent senator, while Markey has argued his “experience is not the opposite of change.”

Ocasio-Cortez lauded Markey’s legislative record on issues like affordability and clean energy, citing their work together on the Green New Deal in Congress.

“At a time when powerful special interests are making life harder for everyday Americans, Massachusetts working families need a champion in the U.S. Senate to stand up for them and fight corporate greed,” Ocasio-Cortez said in a statement .

“Ed Markey has spent his career doing exactly that, from our partnership on the Green New Deal to running his campaign without accepting a dime of corporate PAC money,” she continued. “His work is an inspiration to many of us who are committed to building a better future for all, and that’s why I’m proud to endorse him.”

Markey and Moulton will face off in a final debate Thursday evening ahead of the primary election on Sept. 1.

The incumbent senator thanked Ocasio-Cortez for her support in a statement Thursday morning. Markey is also backed by progressives like Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elizabeth Warren (Mass.).

“We introduced the Green New Deal to tackle the climate crisis, lower costs, and build an economy that works for working people, not corporations and billionaires,” Markey said. “I am incredibly proud to have her endorsement and look forward to continuing to fight alongside her for the livable future we deserve.”

Moulton has garnered support from Democrats like New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill and Reps. Derek Tran (Calif.), Chrissy Houlahan (Pa.), Seth Magaziner (R.I.) and Pat Ryan (N.Y.).

articles.title: Exclusive: US says ‘significant deterioration’ in China’s treatment of detained American academic
articles.summary: Chinese authorities are increasing restrictions on a wrongfully detained American academic, prompting U.S. officials to express alarm about a “significant deterioration” in his treatment, according to sources familiar with the matter. Min Zin, an American citizen who runs a think tank focused on politics in Myanmar, was arrested in China in June. The Trump administration…
articles.body:
Chinese authorities are increasing restrictions on a wrongfully detained American academic, prompting U.S. officials to express alarm about a “significant deterioration” in his treatment, according to sources familiar with the matter.

Min Zin, an American citizen who runs a think tank focused on politics in Myanmar, was arrested in China in June . The Trump administration on Thursday designated him as “wrongfully detained,” a powerful label that makes advocating for his release a top U.S. priority.

The timing of this action is significant. President Trump is expected to welcome Chinese President Xi Jinping for a state visit on Sept. 24.

Advocates say Trump does have an impressive record of freeing Americans jailed abroad — estimated at more than 100 individuals — and non-Americans, to include political prisoners, individuals kidnapped by terrorist organizations and those persecuted for their religion.

Min Zin’s family and friends hope the designation adds increased urgency for his release, raising concern that his detention is at an unknown location, blocking U.S. consular officials from observing his living conditions. They are only able to meet him at a hotel when he is made available by Chinese authorities. During the last visit, Chinese authorities placed Min Zin at the far end of a conference table, making communication difficult and having a chilling effect on the conversation.

Min Zin’s wife, Sylvia Zin, thanked Trump for formally designating her husband as wrongfully detained, and she described the heartache felt from his absence for more than two months — missing a family vacation, his 14-year-old daughter’s first day of high school and her performing in a school concert. She also said the family will likely be apart for Min Zin’s birthday on Sept. 9.

“This will be the first time in her life that our family is broken apart for a birthday,” she said.

Min Zin, who had a 10-year visa to enter China and was a frequent guest in the country for academic conferences, was traveling to Yunnan province at the invitation of a Chinese academic institution. He was detained upon arrival at the airport on June 3. China has accused Min Zin of spying and endangering China’s national security.

Following a recent meeting with Min Zin, U.S. consular officers described increasingly hostile treatment from Chinese authorities, who employed deliberate tactics to disrupt and frustrate conversations to limit the time in which American officials could talk about substantive issues, according to an account of the visit.

Chinese authorities barred U.S. officials from discussing with Min Zin any questions related to his case, interrogation, treatment, work on Myanmar or colleagues. Officials would receive a warning if they violated any of these terms, and a second violation would end the visit immediately.

A consular officer, who has dealt with Americans detained in China for more than two years, called it one of the most disruptive and restrictive visits he’s ever experienced, according to the account.

U.S. officials are also concerned about Chinese authorities restricting humanitarian requests for Min Zin, including blocking reading materials, refusing to provide outside allergy medication — saying that the authorities would provide their own — and a new account from him of knee pain, raising concern of ill treatment. A person familiar with Min Zin said he never had knee pain before. There’s also concern that he is living with constant light, blocking his ability to sleep.

Despite this, officials described Min Zin as mentally resilient and physically stable, maintaining a meditation practice and eating meals provided by authorities, and they said he was preparing himself for an extended imprisonment, requiring endurance and resilience. The interruptions and delay tactics employed by Chinese authorities limited the 30-minute conversation to about 15 minutes, the account estimated, but Min Zin used the time to relay to his family that they prioritize their health and exercise vigilance at home, based on worries about transnational Chinese repression.

The Hill has reached out to the State Department and Chinese Embassy in Washington, D.C., for comment.

Min Zin is a native of Myanmar and participated as a student in the country’s 1988 democracy movement. He studied political science at the University of California, Berkeley and later established in Myanmar an independent think tank, the Institute for Strategy and Policy. He left the country after the military coup in 2021. China is Myanmar’s most powerful and influential neighbor.

Sylvia Zin said her husband traveled to China “in pursuit of academic exchange and because he deeply values the people to people ties that can be built over the sharing of ideas.”

“Min Zin believed that the PRC understood the importance of academic cooperation, but the arrest of an American academic sends the opposite message,” she said.

A U.S. official told Reuters that Min Zin’s detention “has raised grave concerns among other scholars about ​whether they could be ⁠subject to entrapment and detention by China,” hitting on a pressure point for Beijing as they look to increase people-to-people ties and academic exchange with the U.S.

“The safety and security of U.S. citizens globally is President Trump’s top priority, and the president has been clear that China must treat U.S. citizens with respect — and those wrongfully detained or under exit bans must be released,” the official said.

Min Zin is the second American considered “wrongfully detained,” following the arrest in 2024 of Youlin Chen, a Chinese-born American seismologist. He was designated in March, and his case was made public in July. House lawmakers have cited human rights groups saying an estimated 200 Americans are detained in China, including under exit bans that prevent them from leaving the country.

Trump raised Chen’s case with Xi when the two met in Beijing in May , and the Chinese leader committed to look into it, according to a source familiar with the matter, but the family has received no indication that Chen’s case is being considered.

But in an extraordinary move last month, China released Ezra Jin, a Chinese Christian pastor whose daughter is American, after Trump raised his detention with Xi.

articles.title: David Jolly: ‘I don’t care about the left-right spectrum’
articles.summary: Florida’s Democratic nominee for governor, David Jolly, said Wednesday he’s not focused on the political divide within the party but rather is seeking solutions to big-ticket issues impacting voters ahead of the midterm elections. “I’m in a very postpartisan, postideological space. articles.body:
Florida’s Democratic nominee for governor, David Jolly, said Wednesday he’s not focused on the political divide within the party but rather is seeking solutions to big-ticket issues impacting voters ahead of the midterm elections.

“I’m in a very postpartisan, postideological space. I reject the left-right spectrum. I don’t care about the left-right spectrum. We have big problems that need big solutions. So what I did as a Democrat is amplify the fundamental values in our party, that the economy should work for everybody,” Jolly said during a Wednesday appearance on NewsNation’s “Cuomo.”

“Economic growth is good, but it’s got to work for everybody. The private sector should lead, but government needs to fill in the gaps,” he added.

Jolly served in the House as a Republican before becoming an independent in 2019 following woes with President Trump.

Last year, he registered as a Democrat and launched his gubernatorial bid within a new party.

His campaign has coincided with a growing progressive pulse within the faction focused on improving healthcare, housing, safety and the environment, which Jolly has said are of concern to all people.

The Democratic gubernatorial nominee firmly stated he was a capitalist in favor of the private economy and rejected ties to socialism during the “Cuomo” segment.

However, he said democratic socialists including Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon (D) are gaining momentum by outlining a plan to address the economic crisis impacting Americans nationwide.

“Our politics are very different. We disagree on a whole lot,” Jolly said of Nixon and democratic socialists.

“But the reality is, I think in each one of these races, to your point, Democratic candidates were addressing the economic crisis that is real. That is real,” he added.

Jolly continued to state that Republicans’ “major fault” is refusing to recognize the economic anxiety.

“They’re following the Trump playbook of just telling people that what they’re feeling is wrong. Republicans are out of touch. Democrats have an opportunity this year,” he added.

Jolly will face off against Trump endorsed Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) in November, while Nixon is challenging Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.) for her seat in the upper chamber.

articles.body:
Former Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson (R) called a recent private memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) about data centers “alarmist in tone.”

Appearing on NewsNation, Hutchinson told host Blake Burman, “The NRSC memo was almost alarmist in tone, which is concerning in and of itself.”

“Republican candidates need to define themselves on the issue of data centers and their expansions and building them in our communities before they are defined on it and before it becomes a bigger issue,” Hutchinson continued.

The NRSC memo, titled “ Ohio Data Center Risk ,” was sent to AI companies, arguing if incumbent Ohio Sen. Jon Husted (R) loses his Senate election against former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) — who the memo says has made opposition to data centers the “centerpiece of his campaign against Husted” — the campaign against data centers “will expand far beyond Ohio.”

The NRSC wrote that these companies should make a better case for themselves and do it fast: explaining who benefits, who pays for higher costs and why communities should want data centers.

Some polling shows that data centers are broadly unpopular with a majority of Americans: 41 percent surveyed by Public First in July said they would oppose a data center being built near them.

Burman asked Hutchinson if he believed this movement against data centers would cause Republicans to align with Democrats as the 2026 midterms approach.

“I think they’ll be very careful in what they say. They will support data centers as long as there is local control, as long as the residential consumers don’t pay for the electricity, they pay their own way,” he said.

Hutchinson cited widespread concern from Americans on the water and energy consumption of data centers as to why data centers may be unpopular in Ohio.

Hutchinson acknowledged that data centers had been seen as “an attractive opportunity for governors to compete and to bring these data centers in,” but “now it becomes a controversial issue that you better be able to articulate clearly that you don’t want consumers to be paying for it and harmed.”

Hutchinson also mentioned President Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, which more than 300 companies have signed on to since it was announced in March. It requires companies involved in building data center infrastructure to cover the entire energy costs .

EdgeCore Digital Infrastructure, a data center developer operating in California and Virginia, became the latest company to sign the pledge on Aug. 13 .

articles.title: To outcompete China, unhandcuff America’s biotech innovators
articles.summary: Former official David Mansdoerfer argues that bureaucratic delays at the FDA threaten American leadership in the growing regenerative medicine sector and give international competitors like China a strategic advantage.
articles.body:
America’s long-held dominance in biotechnology is slowly slipping away . China now conducts more clinical drug trials than the U.S. , and its share of global drug-development activity has grown dramatically over the past decade.

This is a problem that goes well beyond the biotech industry. The countries that can discover, develop, manufacture and commercialize the next generation of medical breakthroughs will have an enormous advantage in economic competitiveness, national security and public health.

But America still has opportunities to outcompete China, and regenerative medicine could be one of them. Regenerative treatments involve biotechnologies such as engineered tissues, biomaterials, and gene editing that seek to repair or replace damaged cells, tissues and organs. While China is active in the field , the market for this technology in the U.S. is expected to balloon to $90 billion by 2030.

The U.S. can outpace the rest of the world in this next frontier of healthcare, but only with a policy environment that encourages innovation and enables American companies to compete on equal footing with their global counterparts. That requires a nimble and dynamic regulatory process — one that makes timely decisions and gives innovators the certainty they need to create products that meet patient needs.

The consequences of delayed regulatory decisions are not hypothetical. One Florida biotechnology company has spent years living them.

Based in Pensacola, Regenative Labs develops products for patients derived from donated human birth tissue. Although patients and physicians across the U.S. have benefited from Regenative’s cutting-edge biotech, the company can’t serve patients overseas. That’s because the FDA won’t make a decision on the company’s applications for a Certificate of Foreign Government, a document needed to sell to foreign markets. For three years, dating back to the Biden administration, the company has been mired in bureaucratic delay , waiting endlessly for a decision that federal law requires the FDA to make within 20 days.

While bureaucrats have dithered, foreign competitors unbound by the FDA’s rules have gained a leg up and a chunk of market share abroad. The easy solution for Regenative would be to pack up and move its operations offshore, but it wants to stay and grow in Florida, where it began. An American company with American-developed technology has been put at a competitive disadvantage and held back from expanding its workforce, not because of a lack of demand for its products, but because bureaucrats have ignored their congressional mandate to act.

This case is about more than one company’s export applications. It demonstrates how regulatory inaction can limit biotech growth, slow manufacturing, and weaken America’s position in one of the world’s fastest-growing industries. Every delayed decision is a missed opportunity for American workers, domestic manufacturing, and the homegrown companies developing the next generation of medical innovation.

The situation reflects a broader reality. Biotechnology is rapidly becoming one of the defining industries of the 21st century. The countries that discover, develop and produce tomorrow’s medical breakthroughs will shape the future and come out on top. Maintaining American leadership in biotech means ensuring that pipeline journey happens here at home.

The U.S. has long been the world’s standard bearer in medical innovation, but that status is in jeopardy. China has its sights on overtaking us as the global leader in biotech. We cannot take our leadership in this arena for granted. Every time unnecessary bureaucracy hamstrings American innovators while competitors abroad move ahead, we risk surrendering a strategic advantage that has taken half a century to build.

The benefits of American biotechnology extend far beyond commercial markets and America’s borders. American-developed medical innovations have the potential to improve care for hundreds of thousands of U.S. service members, military families and other Americans living overseas. Why would we prevent America’s service men and women and their families abroad from accessing new treatments that could improve their health?

Making America Healthy Again isn’t just about discovering new ways to be healthy. It’s about creating conditions that allow innovation to reach patients. Our regulatory system must provide the clarity American companies need to succeed. Transparency and timely action from our agencies are as important as anything else to advancing better health and preserving U.S. leadership in biotechnology for years to come.

David Mansdoerfer is the former Deputy Assistant Secretary for Health and currently serves as an adjunct professor in health policy and politics at Pepperdine University School of Public Policy.

Minnesota state House Speaker Lisa Demuth (R) beat Lindell by 11 percentage points, but Lindell has refused to cede to the lawmaker, citing concerns with voting machines…
articles.body:
MyPillow founder Mike Lindell said Wednesday he’s prepared to spend “upwards of $1 million” for a private recount of ballots cast in the Minnesota Republican primary for governor.

Minnesota state House Speaker Lisa Demuth (R) beat Lindell by 11 percentage points, but Lindell has refused to cede to the lawmaker, citing concerns with voting machines and election integrity.

“Even if this recount and audit does not overturn my election for governor of Minnesota, I believe this is the gateway to getting rid of these electronic voting machines,” Lindell wrote in a Tuesday press release .

The MyPillow founder has railed against voting machines since President Trump lost the 2020 election.

Lindell pushed to overturn the election six years ago and is now offering to pay for a full hand recount and audit of this year’s Republican primary for Minnesota’s governorship.

Costs are projected to reach $825,000, as outlined by the Minnesota secretary of State.

But Lindell says he’s prepared to spend more to hire a team of workers to oversee the state’s recount.

He faces a Monday deadline to turn in “a bond, cash or surety,” as reported by NBC News .

Lindell told the outlet he plans to “personally go in there” himself to deliver the official request Monday.

Lindell owes electronic voting system Smartmatic $56,369 in sanctions as the result of a ruling in a defamation lawsuit brought against the executive for casting doubt on the company’s election technology.

Because he refused to pay, he was held in civil contempt, racking up an additional $500 daily fine, which his lawyers say he can’t afford.

On Wednesday, Lindell’s attorneys sent a letter to U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Bryan to file a motion to reconsider the ruling holding him liable for defamation.
